summary: Earth Jukebox turns NASA Earth visualizations into music in real time, right in the browser. A playhead sweeps across a NASA visualization (video or image). For each thin vertical slice it measures how warm, cold, green and sharp the area is, and plays five voices from those numbers: melody, bass, pad, sparkle and rhythm. Notes come from a chosen musical scale, so it always sounds in tune, and the same picture always sounds the same. Users can let it sweep on its own or explore any spot with a mouse, a finger or the arrow keys, and the app describes what is on screen out loud. It makes Earth science available through hearing: it helps people who cannot see maps well and makes slow changes easier to notice.
details:
What it does: Earth Jukebox pairs NASA visualizations with real-time sonification. The picture is cut into 48 vertical slices. A playhead reads one slice at a time and measures five simple things from its colours: warmth, coldness, greenness, edge sharpness and the most striking spot. Each number drives one voice. The most striking spot sets the melody pitch (higher on the picture = higher note), cold areas lower the bass, warm areas lift the pad chord, green areas trigger short sparkle notes and sharp edges make the rhythm louder. All notes are quantised to a musical scale, so the result always stays in tune and the same picture always sounds the same.

How people use it: Sweep mode plays the picture automatically. Explore mode lets you move over any spot with a mouse, finger or arrow keys and hear it. A built-in library of NASA visualizations has search, topic and region filters, shuffle and auto-play next. Moods and scales change the character of the sound. The app speaks a short plain-language description of what is on screen, so it works for people who cannot see the map. A Sources panel collects every NASA visualization that was played and copies the list in one click.

Benefits and impact: Earth science is almost always shown as pictures. Sound adds a second channel: it helps blind and low-vision people, and makes slow changes (forests, night lights, ocean temperature) easier to notice.

Tools: a single web page, plain JavaScript and the Web Audio API (oscillators, FM synthesis, filters, convolution reverb, delay), no third-party libraries and no server.

Honest limits: the sound is built from the colours of NASA's visualizations, not from the raw satellite bands. Using real spectral data (for example Landsat or MODIS) is our next step, together with tests with blind and low-vision users.
